**Author:** Daniel Antal \| **ORCID:** [0000-0001-7513-6760](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7513-6760) \| **Google Scholar:** [Daniel Antal](https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=Is3IOGEAAAAJ) \| **Contact:** [Reprex](https://reprex.nl/contact/)

This working paper presents the **Dēliņi Farmstead demonstrator** as an applied implementation of the Heritage Digital Twin Ontology (HDT-O) and situates it within a wider research programme on human-centric semantic knowledge production. It examines how heterogeneous museum, archival, bibliographic, linguistic, and photographic evidence can be transformed into reviewable claims, maintained as structured knowledge in Wikibase, and projected into an HDTO-compliant Heritage Digital Twin.

The methodological foundations are developed in a set of companion working papers. **Semantic Knowledge Production** distinguishes candidate assertions from stabilised semantic states and treats semantic authority as the outcome of explicit, provenance-bearing transitions [@antal_semantic_knowledge_production_2026]. **The Review Algebra** formalises candidate generation, human review, finalisation, and recursive semantic stabilisation over atomic assertions [@antal_review_algebra_2026]. **Betwixt** provides the computational implementation of human review through relational review projections [@antal_betwixt_2026], while **Bounded Federation** develops the corresponding graph-to-graph approach for purpose-directed, reviewable semantic exchange between independently governed knowledge graphs [@antal_bounded_federation_2026].

The present paper complements these methodological and computational papers by asking how their concepts operate in a concrete **Heritage Digital Twin**. The Dēliņi demonstrator therefore serves both as an implementation case study and as practical feedback on HDTO 1.1: it tests the relationship between heritage entities and their digital twins, proposition sets and maintenance activities, digital representations and evidence, overlapping inspection contexts, and the operational mapping between HDTO and Wikibase.

Together, these working papers develop complementary conceptual, formal, computational, federation, and applied heritage components of the same research programme. They should therefore be read as companion papers rather than successive versions of a single manuscript.

This manuscript is a working paper and has not undergone peer review. Its HDTO implementation patterns and recommendations are presented for discussion and may be revised in response to further implementation experience and feedback from the HDTO and cultural heritage research communities.

# Introduction

On **10 July 2026**, we visited the **Latvian Ethnographic Open-Air Museum** (Latvijas Etnogrāfiskais brīvdabas muzejs, LEBM) in Riga to document the reconstruction history of the **Dēliņi Farmstead**. Following discussions with the museum staff, we selected the main farmhouse as a compact but representative case study for demonstrating how museum collections, archival records, library resources, and multilingual heritage knowledge can be brought together into a single interoperable digital twin.

![](png/delini/delini_flowchart_1.png){fig-align="center"}

```{=html}
<!---
Field inspection
        │
        ▼
Photographic observations
        │
        ▼
Semantic review
        │
        ▼
Wikibase
        │
        ▼
Representative Commons image
        │
        ▼
Heritage Digital Twin
--->
```

This working paper has three complementary purposes. First, it presents the *Dēliņi Farmstead* as an executable implementation of the Heritage Digital Twin Ontology (HDTO). Second, it uses that implementation as the basis for a cooperation proposal with the *Latvian Ethnographic Open-Air Museum* and future European heritage initiatives. Third, it provides practical implementation feedback to the *ECHOES technical team* by demonstrating how HDTO can be operationalised within everyday museum practice and identifying implementation patterns that may support wider adoption of the ontology.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Observational and Data Aquisition

The main farmhouse consists of four principal spaces:

- master bedroom,

- living room,

- kitchen,

- anteroom.

Our objective was not to create a complete inventory of the farmstead but to construct a small, reviewable digital twin that demonstrates semantic interoperability across different cultural heritage domains.

The observational corpus is organised into four top-level collections, each representing a distinct professional domain.

### Farmstead (Museum collections)

This folder contains our photographic observations of the reconstructed buildings and selected museum artefacts.

![](png/delini/delini_artefacts_example.png)

```{=html}
<!---
Farmstead/
     building_1/
         artefacts/
           leather_shoe/
            sash/
            large_spoon/
          details/
            living_room/
            kitchen/
            master_bedroom/
            roof/
      granary/
--->
```

The artefacts are intentionally separated from the rooms. Although, for example, the leather shoe is displayed in the living room, it is not yet known whether it originally belonged to the Dēliņi Farmstead. Separating artefacts from architectural spaces avoids introducing unsupported semantic assumptions at the observational stage.

The photographs document both the reconstructed building and architectural details that are relevant for understanding the reconstruction process, such as roof construction.

These observations naturally lend themselves to representation using **CIDOC CRM**, or its heritage digital twin profile **HDTO**, where buildings, rooms, architectural elements and museum objects are described according to museum documentation practice.

Our primary focus is `farmhouse (dzīvojamā māja)`. We included only a small number of photographs of `granary (klēts)`, together with overview photographs of `farmhouse (dzīvojamā māja)`, `granary (klēts)`, and `granary and cart shed (klēts - ratnīca)`, to demonstrate that the model naturally scales beyond a single building. The same approach can be extended to the entire Dēliņi Farmstead, to all Livonian buildings reconstructed within the Latvian Ethnographic Open-Air Museum, and ultimately to related collections held by other institutions, such as the Ventspils Seaside Open Air Museum. In the demonstrator we will illustrate this interoperability by incorporating one reconstructed building from Ventspils.

This illustrates the value of heritage digital twins. Researchers can investigate the documentary, architectural, and material evidence relating to Livonian buildings across multiple institutions without physically visiting geographically dispersed collections or repeatedly handling often fragile archival records and museum objects. Rather than replacing the physical collections, the digital twin provides an interoperable, reviewable representation that supports research, comparison, and semantic enrichment while preserving the authority of the original collections.

### Folio (Archival collections)

The second collection contains photographic reproductions of archival documentation consulted during the museum visit.

![](png/delini/delini_folder_structure.png)

```{=html}
<!---
Folio/
    Box_1/
        Folder_1/
        Folder_2/
        Photo_envelope/
    Box_2/
        Folder_3/
        Folder_4/
--->
```

The archival material documents different phases in the history of the farmstead.

- **Box 1** primarily contains documentation relating to the identification, documentation, and dismantling of the original buildings on the Livonian coast. It contains Folder 1, Folder 2, and a photo envelope with historical photographs.

- **Box 2** primarily documents the transport, reconstruction, and subsequent maintenance of the buildings within the museum.

The archival hierarchy closely resembles a conventional archival arrangement described using **ISAD(G)**, with description generally stopping at folder level while selected photographs and documents receive item-level description.

For the purposes of interoperability, however, we model these materials using **RiC-O**, whose graph-based model provides considerably richer connections with museum collections and other documentary resources.[^1]

[^1]: *Records in Contexts–Conceptual Model* and *Ontology* [@RiC-CM_1_0]

This choice reflects the institutional context of the Latvian Ethnographic Open-Air Museum. Although its primary mission is museological rather than archival, it naturally maintains an operational archive documenting the acquisition, reconstruction, conservation, and maintenance of its buildings and collections. Such records are essential for understanding the provenance of the reconstructed farmsteads, yet they are often managed separately from the museum collections that they document.

Using RiC allows these operational records to remain archivally coherent while connecting them directly to museum objects described with CIDOC CRM or HDTO. At the same time, the RiC representation can be linked naturally to archival records held by the National Archives of Latvia, the Latvian Folklore Archive, and other archival institutions without requiring the museum to reorganise its collections according to archival principles.

Many museums periodically transfer records of permanent historical value to professional archives, while archival institutions increasingly support museums through digitisation programmes and digital preservation services. Adopting an archival conceptual model for documentary evidence therefore improves interoperability across the wider cultural heritage ecosystem without changing the museum's primary collection management practices.

Traditionally, these archival materials are consulted on site by visiting researchers alongside the museum collections. In this demonstrator, we instead construct a reviewable digital representation that enables researchers to investigate the relationships between museum objects, archival records, and published documentation through a single interoperable knowledge graph while preserving the provenance and authority of each source.

### Bibliography (Library resources)

The third collection contains documentary resources relevant to the farmstead.

Rather than downloading documents or manually copying bibliographic metadata, we created a **WACZ** web archive containing stable snapshots of selected resources, including

- an OPAC record from the Latvian National Library;
- a blog article describing the ethnographer who documented the Dēliņi Farmstead;
- educational material introducing Livonian culture through activities taking place in the reconstructed farmhouse.

These resources naturally follow **Dublin Core** bibliographic practice while remaining reproducible through web archiving.

Our approach extends the use of WACZ beyond conventional web archiving. We use WACZ files as reproducible acquisition packages that preserve both the retrieved resources and the context in which they were observed. This provides several advantages.

- **Reproducible acquisition.** WACZ files preserve authoritative snapshots of bibliographic records and web resources exactly as they were observed, independently of the underlying library or content management system.

- **Provenance.** The capture records when and from where each resource was retrieved, allowing the provenance of bibliographic metadata and associated web resources to be reconstructed and reviewed.

- **Heterogeneous sources.** WACZ allows bibliographic records, institutional websites, blogs, educational materials, and other web resources to be collected using the same reproducible workflow. In this demonstrator, for example, the Livones.net website provides valuable contextual information despite not being represented as a conventional bibliographic resource.

The resulting WACZ files become observational archives of documentary evidence. Using **fscontext**, both conventional library resources and other web-based documentary materials can be organised into a common contextual collection and subsequently reviewed using the same semantic workflow. The result is a lightweight cross-domain catalogue that integrates library metadata with other documentary resources without requiring the participating institutions to adopt a common library system.

### Language

The final collection contains a small multilingual reference vocabulary describing the concepts required by the demonstrator.

Rather than attempting to build a complete dictionary, this collection provides the minimal terminology required to describe the buildings, rooms, architectural elements, artefacts, and surrounding landscape.

The vocabulary includes English, Latvian, Livonian, and, where relevant, Russian representations. It may be implemented using **Wikibase Lexemes**, providing a lightweight operational implementation of **OntoLex-Lemon** sufficient for multilingual annotation and text generation.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Building an Interoperable Heritage Digital Twin

The Dēliņi demonstrator combines four complementary knowledge domains, each described using the conceptual model that is most appropriate for its professional community.

| Collection   | Primary conceptual model         |
|--------------|----------------------------------|
| Farmstead    | HDTO / CIDOC CRM                 |
| Folio        | RiC-O                            |
| Bibliography | Dublin Core                      |
| Language     | OntoLex-Lemon / Wikibase Lexemes |

Our objective is not to replace these conceptual models with a universal ontology. Instead, each domain retains its own conceptualisation while interoperability is established through semantic review and a shared operational knowledge graph.

Each reviewed heritage subject is represented as a Wikibase item that serves as the operational representation of the subject within the demonstrator. The corresponding semantic descriptions remain expressible in their native conceptual models, allowing the resulting knowledge graph to interoperate with museum, archival, bibliographic, and linguistic information systems.

Observations—including photographs, archival reproductions, and WACZ captures—provide the evidential basis for semantic review. The review process establishes explicit correspondences between the participating domains using a small operational vocabulary linking heritage objects, archival records, bibliographic resources, and multilingual concepts.

The resulting knowledge graph is therefore not a new universal ontology but a semantic integration layer that preserves the authority of each contributing domain while making their relationships explicit and reviewable.

:::
The documentation of the farmstead shows some advantages and some dilemmas of using Heritage Digital Twins. This document aims to provide a feedback to the developers of the HDT Ontology and to the LEBM.

![](png/delini/farmstead_organisation.png)

```{=html}
<!---

Farmstead
    ├── Main house
    │      ├── Living room
    │      │       └── Woven sash
    │      ├── Kitchen
    │      └── Bedroom
    └── Barn
--->
```

Currently HDT-O creates new subclasses of CIDOC, the conceptual model and ontology for museums without guidance on use for other heritage objects that are stored in archives and libraries. The LEBM is an excellent case study, because its collection has both museum artefacts and archival records, and it publishes books and other bibliographical objects.

Our suggested implementation of the HDT-O is influenced by RiC-O, which is itself a CIDOC-inspired model for archives. RiC is particularly helpful with leaving the level of description flexible, using Records as the central object, and any combination of records as a `Record set` while any part of the record is a `Record part`. For example, if a carton paper holding two black-and-white photographs (as in our Box 1 - Folder 3) example, each of the two photographs can be described as `record part` and a single carton in the folder as a `record`. Then, new record sets can be created with subgroupings of records for `Folder 3`, or thematically regrouping Folder 3 and Folder 1/2 or other records. This organisation is rather similar to the HDT and its components.

We believe that a HDT digital twin should offer "a level of description" that is in fact a level of inspection: a digital representation of details, artefacts, records, bibliographic material that should be studied together in a single digital environment. We believe that the HDT class is therefore similar to a `record set`, which is in itself a contextualised, curated (sub)collection of records, regardless of their origin, physical storage.

Taking this parallel to CIDOC, it requires judgement if we believe that a single Thing (artefact), or a set of them should make a digital twin.

Let's make this problem more concrete with the Dēlini farmstead. The farmstead is a collection of built structures: buildings, a well, fences. Digital twins in architecture usually relate to a building, and we believe that it is a logical first step to create an inspection area. But what is a building. Our `farmhouse (dzīvojamā māja)` has many details or parts: a living room, a master bedroom, a kitchen, a built-in oven, a roof, a main entrance door, the door has a lock. And it is a display area of artefacts that originally were in use in the house, or a curator saw that such an artefact could have been in use, though the actual artefact comes from different Northern Kurzeme collections. For example, we describe a large spoon next to the oven, or a sash on display in the master bedroom.

The level of inspection is not an intrinsic property of the heritage object but a curatorial decision. The same sash may participate simultaneously in the digital twin of the main farmhouse, in a thematic inspection of Livonian tablet-woven sashes, and in an object-level digital twin devoted exclusively to its material analysis. Our Wikibase implementation supports these overlapping inspection contexts by representing each reviewed heritage subject as a single graph node linked through explicit semantic relationships rather than nested hierarchies.

From the museum's perspective, each object that has an individual inventory number is the unit of description in the inventory book. If we treat the `farmhouse (dzīvojamā māja)` as the unit of inspection, i.e., the subject of the digital twin, then the rooms, the roof, and possibly the artefacts in the `farmhouse (dzīvojamā māja)` are HDT-O components. It would be logical to make the sash in the master bedroom and the large spoon and the leather shoes found next to the living room components, too.

Yet, the `sash` could be inspected among the sashes of LEBM collection, or the `leather shoe` among its footware, and the `big spoon` among the household objects. In RiC-O, we could easily create new contextual, curated sets of their records, and we can do this in CIDOC, too. And, if we wanted to, we could make a HDT-O for a single sash as well. We could place it into a digital inspection area where its fabric could be examined under microscopical photographs, or small samples of its fabric and dye inspected with chemical analysis.

In fact, we do not see that a digital twin has a natural 'level of inspection' the way an archival record usually has a natural level of description (a single record, a folder in a box of records, the box itself)

Our implementation in Wikibase allows to stage different inspection areas. We can imagine the individual buildings of the Dēlini Farmstead as digital twins, but we can equally support the inspection of a collection of sashes or a single sash. This requires a solid collection theory and mereology that should be represented consistently in HDT-O. What is the relationship of HDT objects that belong to a single farmstead? What is the relationship of HDT Objects that can potentially be represented in a HDT object but also as components of others?

#### Details

The details depict well-identifiable constituent parts of the building. If we treat the building as the unit of description, these details are parts of the building. We organise the details into five sets: the `door`, the `oven`, the `roof`, which are built-in, not detachable parts of `farmhouse`. We created photographs in the `master bedroom` and the `living room`. These parts of the building also contain movable artefacts, various ethnographical objects.

::: {#tbl-living-room-detail}

#### Artefacts

We chose four artefacts from the house. While currently they are on display in the house, and for a visitor or researcher they appear to be a part of the house, it is not clear if the objects were moved together from the farmstead, or were collected elsewhere in Northern Kurzeme.

The distinction between a detail and an artefact is that the artefact itself is a unit of description, and has its own inventory number.

# Implementing HDTO in the Dēliņi Demonstrator

The Dēliņi demonstrator provides a concrete environment in which the classes and properties of the Heritage Digital Twin Ontology (HDTO) can be interpreted operationally. Before discussing limitations or possible extensions of HDTO, we first describe the implementation pattern that we use for the demonstrator. The purpose of this section is therefore constructive rather than critical: wherever HDTO already provides an appropriate class or relationship, we use it directly; complementary models are introduced only where the implementation requires semantics that HDTO does not itself provide.

### Human-centric semantic knowledge production

Our general methodology is **human-centric semantic knowledge production**. In simple terms, we do not assume that information found in a photograph, document, database or produced by an automated process is correct just because a computer can turn it into structured data.

We call the material that we use to examine what we know **evidence**. Evidence can be a photograph, an archival record, a museum catalogue, a database record, a publication, or another resource that a curator can inspect. Evidence, just like **data**, is not itself accepted knowledge: it must be interpreted to produce new knowledge. It provides the basis on which statements can be proposed and examined. Different pieces of evidence may support the same statement, contradict it, or leave the question unresolved.

An **atomic statement** is the smallest statement that we ask a curator to consider as one question. It says one thing about one subject: for example, **this object — is a — sash**, or **this photograph — depicts — the Dēliņi farmhouse**. We represent such a statement as **subject — predicate — value**. Calling it *atomic* does not mean that the statement is simple or certainly true; it only means that, for the purpose of the review, we treat it as one statement that can be examined and decided on independently. We call an atomic statement presented for consideration a **claim**, because the purpose of the review is to establish whether that statement holds up to scrutiny. Both humans and computers are fallible: each can make mistakes, but they can also help identify and correct the other's mistakes. Human-centric semantic knowledge production therefore keeps people in control while making deliberate use of computational assistance.

Evidence, existing knowledge, and computational processes can give us **candidate claims**: suggestions about what something is, what it depicts, where it belongs, or how it is related to something else. A human curator remains in control of what becomes accepted knowledge. The curator can accept a claim, reject it when it is wrong, or defer it when there is not enough evidence to decide. We keep a record of the evidence used, who made the decision and when. Only reviewed and accepted claims become part of the **stabilised knowledge** that can safely be used as the basis for further research, inference or publication decisions.

![You can read the current working paper on semantic knowledge production at <https://zenodo.org/records/22099068>. The underlying computational algebra is described at <https://zenodo.org/records/22091484>.](png/semantic_knowledge_production/fig_candidate_semantic_tensor_to_stabilised_domain_state_delini.png){fig-align="center"}

The figure walks through this methodology using four real examples from the Dēliņi case study—a farmhouse, a sash, a bed and an archival photographic record—together with a fictitious person, used so that we can demonstrate questions involving living people without creating personality-rights concerns.

The examples deliberately include mistakes and uncertainty.

- A candidate claim may, for example, wrongly classify the photographed sash as a building; the curator *rejects* that claim and it does not enter the stabilised knowledge.
- Another question may remain unresolved and is therefore *deferred* rather than guessed.
- Once claims have been *reviewed*, the accepted knowledge can support further conclusions, while its provenance remains available to show how we know what we claim to know.
- Before an action such as publishing a photograph is taken, relevant rights and policy conditions can also be checked through **normative claims** about what is permitted and what is not.

In the following sections we use this same process to build and maintain the Heritage Digital Twin: evidence and existing knowledge provide the basis for candidate claims, people remain in control of their review, accepted knowledge enters the twin, and rejected or unresolved claims are prevented from silently propagating into it.

### From evidence to reviewable claims

We work with three main sources of evidence:

- **Our own recordings**, such as photographs, RAW image files, sound recordings and video recordings made during fieldwork or documentation.
- **Web archive collections**, particularly WACZ files that preserve web pages, images and other resources together with the context in which we found them.
- **Existing structured data**, such as statements from Wikidata, other Wikibase instances, MuIS or other sources that provide RDF or similarly structured data.

Evidence can therefore be **multimodal**: an image, sound or video recording, text, web page or structured data can all provide evidence. We use R libraries and OpenRefine to extract, organise, reconcile and reshape these different materials into forms that curators can inspect. At this stage we are not trying to put everything into the knowledge graph. We are preparing evidence and candidate claims so that a person can understand what is being proposed and decide what should happen to it.

A curator can review the same material in different **scopes**. First, we may need to make claims about the evidence itself. For example: *Does this JPG belong to our documentation? Is it usable, or is it too blurred? Was it accidentally placed in the wrong folder?* We can then make claims about what the evidence tells us: *Does this photograph depict the museum object with inventory number 8246? Does it depict a person? Is the depicted building the Dēliņi farmhouse?* We call this the **dual review format**: we can review claims about the evidence and claims about the heritage entity represented or documented by that evidence.

This distinction is important. Before we can say where a claim came from, we need to know which evidence was actually used and what that evidence documents. Without establishing these relationships, useful **provenance** becomes difficult: we cannot reliably explain how we came to know something. The same problem appears later when we ask **normative questions**, such as whether a photograph may be published or whether information may be shared with another system. We first need to know which resource we are talking about, what it depicts or documents, where it came from, and which conditions apply to it.

### The Betwixt review workbench

**Betwixt** is our prototype review workbench. The English word *betwixt* means *in between*, which describes its role in the workflow. It complements R and OpenRefine by providing a simple intermediate place where evidence and candidate claims can be presented to a human curator before accepted knowledge is incorporated into the next stabilised state.

The Betwixt workbench turns our general methodology into a practical human review process. The expert does not need to work directly with OpenRefine, complex Excel tables, or RDF-annotated graphs. Evidence and candidate claims are presented in a tabular form, together with short instructions, controlled choices and links to supporting information such as vocabulary definitions or the original source record. Different experts can review different questions: a domain expert may decide what a photograph depicts, a legal expert may review its rights status, and a data steward may decide whether a digital resource is adequate for its intended use.

Betwixt is designed to be simple, serverless, robust and easy to understand. A Betwixt review is generated as a self-contained HTML file containing the JavaScript needed to record the curator's decisions while working in an ordinary web browser such as Chrome, Firefox, Brave or Edge. The review also records the identity and contact information of the reviewer together with the decisions made during the review.

A Betwixt review has three stages. The **original review file** is generated by our system and records what the reviewer was asked to examine. While working, the reviewer can create an **interim version** and return to it later. When the review is complete, a **finalised version** records the reviewer's decisions and the information needed to document who performed the review. Keeping these stages separate allows us to distinguish the candidate material originally presented to the reviewer from the decisions subsequently made about it.

![The top-left panel shows what happens during human review. The bottom-left panel shows the provenance recorded behind the visible workbench. The right-hand panels summarise downstream domain and normative inference; these operations will be examined in the following sections as applications of the digital twin.](png/betwixt/delini_betwixt_semantic_production.png){fig-align="center"}

The workbench is only the visible part of the process. As decisions are made, the system records which evidence was used, what was reviewed, by whom, within which scope, and whether a claim was accepted, deferred or rejected. This provenance accompanies the resulting stabilised knowledge. Only after this human-controlled review can the digital twin use explicit inference rules and symbolic AI to propose further domain conclusions or evaluate normative questions, such as whether a resource may be published. These downstream results are themselves candidate claims rather than unquestionable facts and can therefore return to the review process when human scrutiny is required.

Betwixt can sit between relatively unstructured evidence and more structured data:

**photographs and records → R / OpenRefine → Betwixt review → reviewed tabular data → Wikibase**

It can also sit between two knowledge graphs. Instead of automatically copying everything available from Wikidata or another Wikibase, we select the part that is relevant to our purpose, turn the selected statements into candidate claims, present them for review, and incorporate only accepted claims into our own stabilised knowledge:

**external knowledge graph → bounded selection → Betwixt review → our Wikibase**

We call the latter process **bounded federation**. The aim is not to reproduce another knowledge graph inside our own. External knowledge provides candidate claims that are useful for a particular purpose. We retain information about where those claims came from and allow curators to decide which claims should become part of our own stabilised knowledge.


### From reviewed knowledge to a Heritage Digital Twin

Our next step is to organise the reviewed knowledge as a **Heritage Digital Twin**. For this we use two technologies that play different roles. **HDT-O (Heritage Digital Twin Ontology)** gives us a common language for describing what a heritage digital twin is and how its parts relate to one another. **Wikibase** gives us the database in which we can actually create and maintain these digital twins.

The most important distinction is very simple: **the heritage object and its digital twin are not the same thing**. A farmhouse, sash, photograph or archival record can exist independently of our database. HDT-O calls the heritage entity that we are interested in **HC1 Heritage Entity**. The organised digital knowledge that we maintain about that heritage entity is represented by **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin**. The HC2 is therefore not another name for the physical farmhouse or sash. It is the digital twin through which we describe, connect, review and further enrich what we know about the HC1.

### How this relates to Wikibase

A **Wikibase** is a database organised around **items**. Each item receives a persistent local identifier beginning with `Q`, such as `Q7328`. An item can have a human-readable label and description and a set of structured statements. For example, an item may say that the Dēliņi farmhouse is a farmhouse, that it belongs to a particular farmstead, that it is associated with Livonian heritage, and that it is documented by particular records or photographs.

There is an important duality here. When we look at a Wikibase item such as `Q7328`, most of its statements appear to talk directly about the heritage entity: **the farmhouse — instance of — farmhouse**. But technically the Q-item is a digital dataset maintained in our information system. It can therefore also have information about the digital record itself: where its knowledge came from, when it was reviewed, what evidence supports it, which version is current, or how it may be used. In other words, the same operational Wikibase item gives us an access point to statements **about the heritage entity** and statements **about the digital twin that describes it**.

HDT-O gives us a vocabulary for keeping these two roles conceptually separate:

- **HC1 Heritage Entity** — the thing that the knowledge is about: for example, the Dēliņi farmhouse, a sash, a museum artefact or an archival record.
- **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin** — the organised digital representation through which we maintain knowledge about that heritage entity.

For our implementation, a Wikibase Q-item therefore acts as the **operational anchor of the Heritage Digital Twin**. When a statement describes the farmhouse itself, we interpret it on the **HC1 side** of the model. When we record how the digital knowledge was created, reviewed, maintained or connected to evidence, we are describing the **HC2 side**. The distinction is ontological rather than necessarily a requirement to create two Q-items for everything.

This is why the review process described above matters. We first identify what heritage entity we are talking about and register its digital twin. Betwixt then helps us decide which candidate claims should become part of the twin's stabilised knowledge and records how those decisions were reached. Subsequent enrichment therefore does not mean repeatedly rediscovering the physical object. We are **maintaining and enriching the HC2 digital twin on the basis of evidence about its HC1 heritage entity**.


## Alignment of the Wikibase Ontology and HDT-O

The correspondence between Wikibase and HDT-O is not a one-to-one mapping between database objects and ontology classes. Wikibase provides the **operational data structure** in which we maintain the digital twin, while HDT-O provides the **ontological interpretation** of the entities, statements and activities represented there. We therefore do not need to create a separate Wikibase item for every HDT-O class instance.

The central mapping starts with the Wikibase Q-item that anchors a heritage entity. The same Q-item participates in two closely related roles. Statements such as **instance of — tablet-woven sash** or **located in — Dēliņi farmhouse** can make propositions about the **HC1 Heritage Entity**. Other statements may concern the **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin** itself. Information about how these propositions were established, reviewed, changed and maintained belongs to the provenance of the digital twin and its maintenance. HDT-O therefore allows us to distinguish the subject of a proposition from the proposition's membership in the maintained content of HC2.

HC1 can be further specialised. A physical object such as the Dēliņi sash or farmhouse can be interpreted as an **HC3 Tangible Heritage Entity**. A digital photograph of the sash is not another instance of the sash and does not become part of HC1 merely because we use it as evidence. It can instead be represented as an **HC5 Digital Representation** connected to what it represents. This distinction allows several photographs, records and other digital resources to contribute evidence about the same heritage entity without multiplying the heritage entity itself.

The propositional content maintained by HC2 is organised in HDT-O through **HC16 Heritage Proposition Sets**. Individual HC16 proposition sets are persistent rather than editable: changes in the twin are represented through different proposition sets rather than by modifying the content of an existing HC16. **HP33 contains** relates the HC2 to proposition sets forming its current content, while former proposition sets remain traceable through **HP34 contained** [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

Changes to the twin are represented by **HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance**. An HC11 activity can document an HC1 heritage entity and compose or complement its HC2 digital twin. This provides the HDT-O location for activities through which reviewed knowledge is admitted to, corrected in, or otherwise maintained in the digital twin. Betwixt supplies part of the provenance needed to describe such an activity: the evidence used, reviewer, review scope, decisions and time of review. The subsequent Wikibase update implements the resulting change to the operational twin.

The first implementation mapping is summarised in @tbl-wikibase-hdto-first-mapping. It is intentionally conservative. An HDT-O entity being relevant to our semantic model does **not** automatically imply that it receives its own QID. Whether a photograph, proposition set, maintenance activity or snapshot should become a first-class Wikibase item depends on whether it needs to be independently identified, linked, queried or maintained.

| Implementation concern | Wikibase representation | HDT-O vocabulary | Interpretation in our implementation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Heritage entity | Q-item serving as the practical operational anchor | **HC1 Heritage Entity** | Projected as the HC1 resource represented by the Q-item |
| Physical heritage entity | Q-item with appropriate `instance of` statements | **HC3 Tangible Heritage Entity** | A material heritage entity, such as the Dēliņi farmhouse or tablet-woven sash |
| Heritage Digital Twin | Shares the practical Q-item anchor used in the Wikibase interface; exported as a distinct semantic resource in the HDT-O projection | **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin** | The digital twin concerning the HC1; distinct from HC1 in the HDT-O representation |
| Heritage entity–twin relationship | Generated by the Wikibase–HDT-O projection rather than necessarily stored as a manually maintained Wikibase statement | **HP1 has digital twin / is digital twin of** | Links **HC1 Heritage Entity → HC2 Heritage Digital Twin**. The HDT-O projection explicitly materialises this distinction even where one Wikibase Q-item serves as their common operational anchor. |
| Digital-twin component relationship | Explicit relationship only where one digital twin is modelled as a component of another | **HP3 is digital twin component of / has digital twin component** | Relates **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin → HC2 Heritage Digital Twin**. It should not be inferred automatically from part-whole relationships between the corresponding HC1 heritage entities, nor from temporary participation in the same inspection context. |
| Digital representation | File or external digital resource; Q-item only when independent graph identity is required | **HC5 Digital Representation**; more specifically **HC7 Digital Audiovisual Object** for the photographic example | A digital representation of a heritage entity; the Dēliņi JPG photographs use the more specific audiovisual class |
| Representation relationship | Wikibase representation or depiction statement | **HP22 represents / has digital representation**; more specifically **HP9 is visual representation of / has visual representation** for digital photography | Connects a digital representation with the entity it represents |
| Heritage community | Q-item for the relevant group | **HP15 is heritage of / has original heritage** | For example, the Dēliņi sash is heritage of the Livonians |
| Current structured knowledge | Current accepted Wikibase statements | **HC16 Heritage Proposition Set** | A set of formal propositions forming part of the knowledge maintained by the twin |
| Current twin content | Current Wikibase state, mapped to proposition sets | **HP33 contains / is proposition set of** | Relates HC2 to HC16 proposition sets forming its current content |
| Former twin content | Previous state retained through history or explicit provenance representation | **HP34 contained / is former proposition set of** | Relates HC2 to proposition sets that were previously part of the twin |
| Maintenance of the twin | Betwixt review followed by the corresponding Wikibase update | **HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance** | An activity through which the digital twin is documented, corrected or enriched |
| Heritage entity documented during maintenance | Provenance relationship | **HP18 has documented / was documented by** | Connects an HC11 maintenance activity to the HC1 that it documents |
| Twin affected by maintenance | Provenance relationship | **HP19 has composed / was composed by** | Connects the maintenance activity to the HC2 that it composes or complements |
| Documentary content used | Betwixt provenance and, where required, Wikibase provenance | **HP27 used content of / content was used by** | Relates HC11 maintenance to content of an **E31 Document** used during maintenance; Betwixt's broader `used evidence` relation is not restricted to documentary evidence |
| Content added to the twin | New accepted Wikibase content | **HP30 added content / content was added by** | Records proposition content added through an HC11 maintenance activity |
| Content removed from the current twin | Superseded or withdrawn Wikibase content retained in provenance/history | **HP31 deleted content / content was deleted by** | Records content removed from the current state without treating it as if it had never existed |
| Replacement of content | Version or replacement relationship | **HP32 replaced / was replaced by** | Connects previous proposition content with the content that replaces it |
| Persistent snapshot | Fixed export, release or other persistently identified representation of a changing operational state | **HC14 Volatile Digital Object**, **HC15 Persistent Digital Object** and **HP28 has snapshot** | Treats the operational twin as changing while allowing a particular state to be persistently identified, cited and retrieved |

: First mapping between the operational Wikibase implementation and the HDT-O vocabulary. The mapping is semantic rather than a requirement to create one Wikibase item for every HDT-O entity. {#tbl-wikibase-hdto-first-mapping}

#### Running example: the Dēliņi tablet-woven sash

For the tablet-woven sash, the implementation can initially remain very small. Suppose the sash is represented by Wikibase item `Q123`. Statements such as **Q123 — instance of — tablet-woven sash** and **Q123 — heritage of — Livonians** are propositions about the HC1 heritage entity. Because the sash is a physical object, the HC1 can additionally be classified as HC3 Tangible Heritage Entity.

The photograph `P7101561.jpg` has a different role. Betwixt establishes through review that this particular file depicts the sash. In the HDT-O interpretation, the photograph can therefore be represented as an **HC7 Digital Audiovisual Object**, using **HP9 is visual representation of** to relate it to the photographed sash. HC7 participates in the more general digital-representation pattern represented by **HC5 Digital Representation** and **HP22 represents** [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

The accepted propositions contribute to the knowledge maintained by the sash's HC2 Heritage Digital Twin. In an HDT-O projection, these propositions can be organised into an HC16 Heritage Proposition Set and related to HC2 through HP33. The propositions contained in HC16 need not all have the sash's HC1 resource as their subject: some may describe HC1, while others may concern HC2 or other resources participating in the maintained knowledge.

# Glossary for Revision

The following glossary defines the terms used in this tutorial. Wikibase terms follow the Wikibase Ontology [@wikibase_datamodel]. Heritage Digital Twin terms follow HDT-O 1.1 [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. Where this tutorial introduces an implementation-specific interpretation, this is stated explicitly.

**Accepted claim**\
A candidate claim that has passed the required review and is admitted into the stabilised knowledge used by the Heritage Digital Twin. Acceptance does not imply permanent or universal truth: accepted knowledge may subsequently be reviewed and revised.

**Atomic statement**\
The smallest semantic statement that we ask a reviewer to consider as one question. It says one thing about one subject and is represented in this tutorial as **subject — predicate — value**, or $(s,p,v)$. Calling a statement *atomic* does not mean that it is simple or certainly true; it means that it is treated as one independently reviewable statement.

**Betwixt**\
The prototype human review workbench used in this tutorial. Betwixt presents evidence and candidate claims in a simple tabular form and records the decisions made during review. It acts as an intermediate layer between evidence and structured data prepared with tools such as R and OpenRefine, and the knowledge subsequently maintained in Wikibase.

**Bounded federation**\
A purpose-directed process through which selected knowledge from another knowledge graph is transformed into candidate claims for possible inclusion in the local knowledge graph. Candidate claims are reviewed rather than automatically copied. The source, mapping and review decision remain traceable.

**Candidate claim**\
An atomic statement presented for consideration but not thereby assumed to be correct. A candidate claim can be accepted, rejected or deferred during review.

**Deferred**\
A review outcome indicating that a candidate claim has been examined but that there is presently insufficient evidence or competence to accept or reject it. Deferral is an explicit result and should not be replaced by a guess.

**Digital representation**\
A digital object representing an observable entity, such as a digital photograph of a heritage object. HDT-O represents this concept with **HC5 Digital Representation** [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. A digital representation is distinct from the heritage entity it represents: several photographs can represent the same heritage entity without thereby creating several heritage entities.

**Dual review**\
A Betwixt review arrangement in which claims about an evidence resource and claims about the entity represented or documented by that evidence can be reviewed together while remaining semantically distinct. For example, a reviewer may establish both **this JPG — depicts — this sash** and **this sash — heritage of — Livonians**.

**Evidence**\
Material examined or used when establishing or reviewing a claim. Evidence may be multimodal and can include photographs, sound and video recordings, archival documents, web pages, database records or structured data. Evidence, like data, is not itself accepted knowledge: it must be interpreted to produce knowledge.

**HC1 Heritage Entity**\
The entity regarded as heritage and forming the subject of a Heritage Digital Twin [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In this tutorial, examples include the Dēliņi farmhouse and the tablet-woven sash. HC1 refers to the heritage entity, not to the database record describing it.

**HC2 Heritage Digital Twin**\
A collection of sets of formal propositions concerning an HC1 Heritage Entity [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In this tutorial, HC2 is understood operationally as the organised and changing digital knowledge maintained about an HC1 through our Wikibase-based implementation. HC1 and HC2 are conceptually distinct even where a single Wikibase Q-item acts as their operational anchor.

**HC3 Tangible Heritage Entity**\
An HDT-O subclass of HC1 for tangible heritage entities [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. A physical sash, building or museum artefact can therefore be represented as both an HC1 Heritage Entity and, more specifically, an HC3 Tangible Heritage Entity.

**HC5 Digital Representation**\
An HDT-O class for digital objects that represent observable entities [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In the running example, the JPG photograph of the Dēliņi sash can be represented as an HC5 Digital Representation of the sash.

**HC7 Digital Audiovisual Object**\
An HDT-O class for digital audiovisual objects, including digital photographs [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In the running example, `P7101561.jpg` can be represented more specifically as an HC7 Digital Audiovisual Object, while HC5 Digital Representation provides the more general representation pattern.

**HP9 is visual representation of (has visual representation)**\
The HDT-O property relating a digital audiovisual object to the observable entity of which it is a visual representation [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In the running example, it relates the digital photograph `P7101561.jpg` to the photographed sash.

**HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance**\
An HDT-O activity through which a Heritage Digital Twin is composed, complemented or otherwise maintained while documenting the relevant heritage entity [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In this implementation, a reviewed Betwixt result followed by the corresponding update of Wikibase can contribute to an HC11 maintenance activity.

**HC15 Persistent Digital Object**\
An HDT-O digital object intended to persist and remain identifiable [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. It can be used when a fixed and persistently identified representation or snapshot of a changing Heritage Digital Twin is required.

**HC16 Heritage Proposition Set**\
An HDT-O class representing a persistent set of formally encoded propositions forming content of a Heritage Digital Twin [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. The propositions in the set need not all have HC1 as their subject: they may concern HC1, HC2, or other relevant resources. The identity of an HC16 depends on its complete set of propositions; changing that content therefore produces a new HC16 rather than modifying the existing proposition set. Current and former HC16s allow changes in the knowledge maintained by HC2 to remain traceable.

**Heritage Digital Twin**\
In this tutorial, an organised and maintainable body of digital knowledge concerning a heritage entity. HDT-O formally represents the heritage entity as HC1 and its Heritage Digital Twin as HC2 [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. Our operational implementation uses Wikibase, Betwixt and supporting R tools to create and maintain this knowledge.

**HP1 has digital twin (is digital twin of)**\
The HDT-O property relating an HC1 Heritage Entity to its HC2 Heritage Digital Twin [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. Our implementation does not necessarily materialise this distinction as two separate Wikibase Q-items; it can be recovered through the Wikibase-to-HDT-O mapping.

**HP15 is heritage of (has original heritage)**\
The HDT-O property used to relate a heritage entity to the relevant group [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In the running example, it supports the representation that the Dēliņi sash is heritage of the Livonians.

**HP18 has documented (was documented by)**\
The HDT-O property relating an HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance activity to the HC1 Heritage Entity documented by that activity [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

**HP19 has composed (was composed by)**\
The HDT-O property relating an HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance activity to the HC2 Heritage Digital Twin that the activity composes or complements [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

**HP22 represents (has digital representation)**\
The HDT-O property connecting a digital representation with the observable entity that it represents [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. It provides the HDTO interpretation of relationships such as a reviewed photograph representing a heritage object.

**HP27 used content of (content was used by)**\
The HDT-O property relating a Digital Twin Maintenance activity to content of an **E31 Document** used during that activity [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. It can therefore represent documentary sources used during maintenance, but it should not be treated as equivalent to Betwixt's broader concept of `used evidence`, which can also include non-documentary evidence.

**HP28 has snapshot (is snapshot of)**\
The HDT-O property relating a volatile digital object to a persistent snapshot [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. It can be used when a fixed, identifiable representation of a changing digital twin state is required.

**HP30 added content (content was added by)**\
The HDT-O property recording content added through a Digital Twin Maintenance activity [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. In this tutorial, it can describe the addition of reviewed proposition content to the digital twin.

**HP31 deleted content (content was deleted by)**\
The HDT-O property recording content removed through a Digital Twin Maintenance activity [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. Deletion from the current twin does not require the historical existence or provenance of that content to be forgotten.

**HP32 replaced (was replaced by)**\
The HDT-O property recording the replacement of one content object by another during Digital Twin Maintenance [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. It is useful when corrected or revised proposition content supersedes an earlier version.

**HP33 contains (is proposition set of)**\
The HDT-O property relating an HC2 Heritage Digital Twin to an HC16 Heritage Proposition Set that forms part of its current content [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

**HP34 contained (is former proposition set of)**\
The HDT-O property relating an HC2 Heritage Digital Twin to an HC16 Heritage Proposition Set that formerly formed part of its content [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. It allows previous knowledge states to remain explicitly traceable after the current twin has changed.

**Item**\
A Wikibase entity representing the thing being described and identified by an item identifier, conventionally beginning with `Q`, such as `Q123` [@wikibase_datamodel]. The information stored about an Item belongs to its **ItemDescription**. In this implementation, an Item can serve as the operational anchor for a heritage entity.

**ItemDescription**\
The collection of information stored about a Wikibase Item, including its labels, descriptions, aliases and Statements [@wikibase_datamodel]. The Item represents the thing being described, while the ItemDescription contains the information recorded about it.

**Item identifier (QID)**\
A stable identifier for a Wikibase Item, conventionally written as `Q` followed by a number, such as `Q123` [@wikibase_datamodel].

**Knowledge graph**\
A graph-structured representation in which entities are connected through explicitly represented relationships. Wikibase provides the knowledge-graph infrastructure used for the Heritage Digital Twins in this tutorial.

**Property**\
A Wikibase entity used to describe relationships and attributes in Statements [@wikibase_datamodel]. Properties are identified by property identifiers, conventionally beginning with `P`.

**Provenance**\
Information recording how knowledge was produced or changed, including relevant evidence, activities, agents, times and derivations. In this tutorial, Betwixt records provenance during review, and the resulting provenance supports subsequent maintenance and use of the Heritage Digital Twin.

**Q-item**\
Informal shorthand in this tutorial for a Wikibase Item identified by a QID [@wikibase_datamodel]. See **Item**.

**Qualifier**\
Additional information attached to a Wikibase statement that qualifies the circumstances in which the statement applies [@wikibase_datamodel]. A qualifier modifies or contextualises a statement rather than creating a separate description of the Wikibase item as a whole.

**Rank**\
A Wikibase mechanism for indicating the relative status of statements concerning the same property, including preferred, normal and deprecated ranks [@wikibase_datamodel]. Rank is part of the Wikibase data model and should not be treated as equivalent to Betwixt review outcomes such as accepted, deferred or rejected.

**Reference**\
Structured information attached to a Wikibase statement indicating a source supporting that statement [@wikibase_datamodel]. A Wikibase reference can participate in provenance representation, but the richer provenance of the review activity may additionally record the evidence used, reviewer, scope, time and decision.

**Rejected**\
A review outcome indicating that a candidate claim has been examined and should not enter the resulting stabilised knowledge. Rejection is retained as part of the review provenance rather than silently deleting the fact that the candidate was considered.

**Review**\
The human-controlled process through which candidate claims are examined and a decision is recorded. In this tutorial, Betwixt supports review by allowing a reviewer to accept, reject or defer candidate claims while recording the evidence and circumstances of the decision.

**Stabilised knowledge**\
Reviewed knowledge considered sufficiently reliable for the current purpose to serve as the basis for subsequent work. Stabilisation is purpose-relative and revisable: it does not mean that a statement has become permanently or universally true.

**Statement**\
A Wikibase structure that assigns a Value to a Property and may additionally have Qualifiers, References and a Rank [@wikibase_datamodel]. Statements form part of the ItemDescription of an Item.

**Wikibase**\
The software and data model used in this tutorial to maintain the operational Heritage Digital Twin. Wikibase organises knowledge around entities such as Items and Properties and represents knowledge through structured statements [@wikibase_datamodel].

**Wikibase Ontology**\
The RDF vocabulary used by Wikibase to express its data model when Wikibase entities and statements are represented as RDF [@wikibase_datamodel]. It provides classes and properties for such concepts as Items, Properties, Statements, References and Ranks. The Wikibase Ontology describes the structure of the Wikibase representation; HDT-O supplies the heritage-domain interpretation used in this tutorial.

# Discussion of the HDTO Conceptual Model

## From HDTO to an operational Heritage Digital Twin

HDT-O provides the conceptual model for the Heritage Digital Twin, while Wikibase provides the operational environment in which we maintain its structured knowledge. The two models should not be treated as if their classes were directly interchangeable. HDT-O describes heritage entities, their digital twins, digital representations, proposition sets and maintenance activities. Wikibase provides Items, ItemDescriptions, Properties, Statements and the structures needed to maintain and query them [@echoes_hdto_1-1; @wikibase_datamodel]. Our implementation therefore requires a mapping between the two rather than a one-to-one identification of their classes.

The Dēliņi demonstrator starts from a simple practical requirement. We want to identify a heritage entity, register a digital twin for it, and subsequently maintain knowledge about it. New evidence does not repeatedly create a new description from scratch. It provides material from which candidate claims can be produced, reviewed and, when accepted, incorporated into the maintained knowledge of the twin. This makes the Heritage Digital Twin a continuing object of semantic production rather than a one-time digitisation product.

### HC1, HC2 and the Wikibase operational anchor

HDT-O makes a fundamental distinction between **HC1 Heritage Entity** and **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin**. HC1 is the entity regarded as heritage. HC2 is the Heritage Digital Twin containing formal propositions concerning that entity [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. For example, the tablet-woven sash in the Dēliņi farmhouse is the HC1: it is the heritage entity about which we want to maintain knowledge. The structured digital knowledge maintained about the sash belongs to its HC2.

Wikibase makes a related but different distinction. A Wikibase **Item** represents the thing being described, while its **ItemDescription** contains the information stored about it, including labels, descriptions, aliases and Statements [@wikibase_datamodel]. This is useful for our implementation, but it should not be mistaken for an exact equivalence between `Item = HC1` and `ItemDescription = HC2`. HDT-O and the Wikibase data model have different purposes.

Instead, we use the Wikibase Item as the **operational anchor** of the twin. Suppose the Dēliņi sash is registered as `Q123`. The Item represents the sash, while Statements associated with its ItemDescription can express propositions such as:

**Q123 — instance of — tablet-woven sash**

**Q123 — heritage of — Livonians**

These statements concern the HC1 heritage entity. At the same time, our implementation must be able to establish which propositions currently belong to its HC2, how they entered the twin, which evidence and review activities support them, and how the twin has changed over time.

For this reason, the distinction between HC1 and HC2 is primarily an **ontological distinction**, not by itself an instruction about Wikibase item identity. A single QID can serve as the practical anchor in the Wikibase interface, while implementations remain free to give HC1 and HC2 separate graph identities where this becomes operationally useful. It is possible to export or project the operational data into HDT-O, however, when such a single Wikibase anchor is resolved into two distinct semantic resources: the **HC1 Heritage Entity** and its **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin**, explicitly related through **HP1 has digital twin** [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

Where an HC2, proposition set, maintenance activity or other component requires independent operational identification and querying, it may also require a separately identified graph resource. This is an implementation decision rather than an automatic requirement to expose every HDT-O resource as a manually maintained Wikibase Item.

The relationship can initially be understood as:

**Wikibase Item → operational anchor**

**HC1 → the heritage entity represented by the Item**

**HC2 → the maintained digital twin concerning that HC1**

This allows the everyday Wikibase interface to remain relatively simple while preserving the more precise distinction required by HDT-O.

### Evidence, representations and the HC1/HC2 boundary

The digital twin cannot be maintained without evidence. In the Dēliņi demonstrator, evidence includes our own photographs, archived web resources and structured information obtained from external databases and knowledge graphs. These resources do not automatically become accepted knowledge merely because they have been collected or transformed into structured data.

The tablet-woven sash provides a simple example. We have a JPG photograph showing the sash in the master bedroom of the Dēliņi farmhouse. Before using the photograph to support further claims, we establish through review that the file belongs to the relevant documentation and that it actually depicts the sash. This produces a relationship of the form:

**photograph — represents/depicts — sash**

HDT-O allows the digital photograph to be understood generally as an **HC5 Digital Representation** and, more specifically, as an **HC7 Digital Audiovisual Object**, while the physical sash is an HC1 Heritage Entity and, more specifically, an **HC3 Tangible Heritage Entity** [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. For digital photography, **HP9 is visual representation of** provides the more specific relationship to the represented observable entity, while **HP22 represents** provides the more general representation relationship. The representation and the represented heritage entity therefore remain distinct. Likewise, classification as HC5 or HC7 does not by itself make the digital representation a component of HC2; its participation in the maintained twin must be established through the relevant HDT-O content and maintenance relationships.

This distinction is essential for provenance. A claim such as **sash — heritage of — Livonians** is a proposition about the HC1. The photograph may be evidence used when establishing or reviewing propositions about that HC1, but the photograph is not itself the proposition. Likewise, recording that a curator consulted the photograph during a review is provenance about the production of knowledge, rather than another descriptive property of the sash.

Betwixt therefore supports a **dual review**. A reviewer can make claims about the evidence resource itself and, in the same review environment, make claims about the heritage entity represented by that evidence. For example:

**P7101561.jpg — represents — Q123**

and:

**Q123 — heritage of — Livonians**

can be reviewed together without treating them as statements about the same subject.

This separation gives us the minimum structure required for useful provenance. Before we can state how knowledge about a heritage entity was produced, we must know which resources were actually used as evidence and how those resources relate to the heritage entity. The same separation later becomes necessary for normative reasoning, because the rights or publication conditions applying to a photograph need not be the same as those applying to the heritage object represented in the photograph.

### Human review and semantic stabilisation

HDT-O provides classes and properties for representing a Heritage Digital Twin, but our implementation additionally requires a method for deciding which candidate propositions should enter its maintained knowledge. We use **human-centric semantic knowledge production** for this purpose.

Evidence, existing knowledge and computational processes can generate candidate claims. Candidate generation may involve extraction from files, transformation with R, reconciliation in OpenRefine, inference from existing knowledge, or bounded federation from an external knowledge graph. None of these operations makes a candidate claim true merely by producing it.

Betwixt places these candidate claims in front of an appropriate reviewer. A domain expert can review claims about the heritage entity, a data steward can review the adequacy of digital resources, and a legal expert can review relevant legal or policy claims. Candidate claims can be accepted, rejected or deferred. Rejected claims do not enter the stabilised knowledge, while deferred claims remain explicitly unresolved rather than being guessed.

This creates a simple semantic production cycle:

**evidence and existing knowledge → candidate claims → review → stabilised knowledge**

The stabilised knowledge is the knowledge considered sufficiently reliable for the current purpose. It is not assumed to be permanently true. New evidence or later review may lead to correction or replacement. This fallibility is important for the Heritage Digital Twin: maintaining a twin means not only accumulating statements but also being able to revise them in a controlled and traceable manner.

### HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance

HDT-O provides an explicit place for this continuing activity through **HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance** [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. We interpret HC11 according to its broader maintenance role rather than equating it with any single user interaction or inspection session.

A maintenance activity can be associated with documenting an HC1 Heritage Entity and composing or complementing its HC2 Heritage Digital Twin. This makes HC11 the natural HDTO location for the provenance-bearing activity through which the state of an operational twin is changed.

In our workflow, several operations may contribute to such maintenance. Evidence may first be extracted and organised with R or OpenRefine. Betwixt may then present candidate claims to a reviewer and record the review decisions. Finally, accepted changes are written to Wikibase. These technical steps do not necessarily have to be represented as separate HC11 instances. What matters is that the semantically significant maintenance activity and its relationship to the resulting change remain identifiable.

For the sash example, the maintenance process can therefore be read simply as:

**photograph and existing records → candidate claims → Betwixt review → accepted claims → Wikibase update**

HDT-O allows the resulting maintenance activity to be connected both to the heritage entity it documented and to the digital twin it composed or complemented. **HP18 has documented** relates the maintenance activity to the HC1, while **HP19 has composed** relates it to the HC2 [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

HDT-O also provides properties for describing changes to the twin's content. **HP30 added content**, **HP31 deleted content** and **HP32 replaced** allow maintenance to be represented as more than an undifferentiated database update [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. This is particularly useful for a review-based implementation because correction should not mean silently overwriting the history of the twin.

### HC16 Heritage Proposition Sets and changing twin states

The propositions in an HC16 should not be understood as statements whose subject must always be HC1  [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. HC16 represents proposition content maintained by HC2, while individual propositions may concern different resources. In our implementation, some propositions describe the HC1 heritage entity, while others may describe the HC2 digital twin or other resources relevant to the maintained knowledge. Membership in the proposition set and the subject of a proposition are therefore separate semantic questions.


This has an important consequence for implementation: an **HC16 is not an editable container**. Once created, it represents a fixed proposition set. If its propositional content changes, the result is a new HC16 rather than a modified version of the same HC16 [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

The distinction allows the digital twin to change while both the HC1 heritage entity and earlier HC16 proposition sets remain identifiable. The Dēliņi sash does not become a different physical sash because our knowledge about it changes. Instead, an **HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance** activity can add a new HC16 proposition set and make an earlier HC16 former content of the twin.

HDT-O distinguishes current and former proposition sets. **HP33 contains** relates an HC2 Heritage Digital Twin to an HC16 that is currently valid, while **HP34 contained** relates it to an HC16 that was formerly valid [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. When maintenance replaces content, the former HC16 is not erased: its HP33 relationship is replaced by HP34, preserving referential integrity and the history of the twin. **HP32 replaced** can additionally connect the new HC16 to the proposition set that it supersedes.

Our semantic stabilisation methodology and HC16 should nevertheless not be treated as identical concepts. Betwixt reviews atomic candidate claims and records the decisions and provenance associated with them. Accepted claims can subsequently contribute to an HC16 proposition set maintained by the HC2. The review process explains **why a proposition was admitted**; HC16 describes **propositional content of the twin**.

A simplified lifecycle is therefore:

**candidate claims → review → accepted claims → new HC16 proposition set → current HC2**

When later evidence requires a correction, **HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance** does not edit the existing HC16. It adds a new HC16 and can replace the previous proposition set, which remains identifiable as former content of the HC2. The changing twin is therefore represented by a succession of persistent proposition sets rather than by repeatedly overwriting the same proposition container.

This interpretation gives us a Heritage Digital Twin that is neither a static database record nor an uncontrolled accumulation of statements. It is a changing body of formal propositions whose maintenance can be documented and whose previous states can remain traceable.

### Volatile twins and persistent snapshots

HDT-O additionally distinguishes between changing and persistent digital objects. **HC14 Volatile Digital Object** represents a digital object whose content can change, while **HC15 Persistent Digital Object** represents a persistently identifiable digital object. **HP28 has snapshot** relates a volatile digital object to a persistent snapshot capturing its content at a particular point in time [@echoes_hdto_1-1].

This distinction is particularly useful for our Wikibase implementation. The operational HC2 maintained through Wikibase is a changing digital object: accepted knowledge can be added, corrected or replaced through later maintenance. A particular state of that twin may nevertheless need to be fixed, cited, archived or exchanged reproducibly. Such a state can be represented as a persistent snapshot rather than treating the live Wikibase state itself as immutable.

We therefore distinguish the **current operational twin** from its **persistent snapshots**. HC16 identifies persistent proposition content forming current or former content of the twin, while HC15 and HP28 provide the complementary mechanism for preserving an identifiable snapshot of the changing digital object as a whole. These mechanisms should not be conflated: an HC16 is a Heritage Proposition Set, whereas an HC15 snapshot captures a persistent state of a volatile digital object.

### Wikibase and HDTO as complementary representations

Wikibase and HDT-O consequently perform complementary functions in our architecture. Wikibase provides the operational environment in which people can identify entities, maintain statements, query the graph and connect knowledge across collections. HDT-O provides the semantic vocabulary through which we can state more precisely what the resulting structures mean as parts of a Heritage Digital Twin [@wikibase_datamodel; @echoes_hdto_1-1].

We therefore do not attempt to reproduce every HDT-O class as a Wikibase Item or every HDT-O property as a manually entered Wikibase statement. Some distinctions can be recovered systematically when the operational data are exported or projected into HDT-O. Other entities need explicit graph identity because they must themselves be cited, queried, related or maintained.

This leads to an important implementation principle:

> **Ontological identity does not automatically require Wikibase item identity.**

A heritage object that we intend to describe and maintain normally requires a stable Item. A digital photograph may remain an identified file unless there is a reason to manage it as a first-class graph entity. An HC16 proposition set or HC11 maintenance activity may be generated from structured review and provenance records rather than requiring a curator to create and maintain Q-items manually. The appropriate representation depends on what must remain independently identifiable and queryable.

The result is deliberately layered. Wikibase remains usable as an operational knowledge system, Betwixt provides the human review boundary through which candidate knowledge becomes stabilised, and HDT-O provides the formal representation through which the resulting knowledge can be understood as a maintained Heritage Digital Twin.

This constructive mapping also exposes questions that cannot be answered simply by assigning more HDT-O classes or creating more Wikibase Items. We still need to decide which digital resources deserve independent graph identity, how overlapping heritage entities and their twins relate to one another, where the boundary of a twin should be drawn, and how evidence and provenance should participate in later normative decisions. The Dēliņi implementation makes these questions concrete, and they are considered in the following section.

## Implementation questions exposed by the Dēliņi demonstrator

The mapping above gives us a workable implementation of the main HDT-O concepts, but it also exposes questions that become important as soon as we work with real collections. The Dēliņi demonstrator contains physical heritage objects, photographs made during our own documentation work, digitised archival records, resources preserved from external websites, and structured knowledge obtained from other databases and knowledge graphs. These resources do not all need to become first-class entities in our Wikibase.

The central implementation question is therefore not simply **what can be represented in the graph**, but **what needs to be represented as an independently identified graph entity**. The distinction matters for keeping the digital twin understandable and maintainable. A knowledge graph in which every working file, intermediate representation and review artefact becomes a Q-item would rapidly become difficult to use. At the same time, resources that are necessary for identification, provenance, publication or later reuse cannot simply disappear from the model.

### What belongs in the graph?

Our starting principle is that **ontological identity does not automatically require Wikibase Item identity**. HDT-O may allow us to classify a resource as an HC1 Heritage Entity, HC5 Digital Representation, HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance activity or HC16 Heritage Proposition Set without requiring a curator to create and maintain a separate Q-item for every instance.

A resource should normally receive independent graph identity when we need to make it the subject or object of persistent relationships, identify it independently, query it directly, publish it as part of the digital twin, or maintain information about it over time. The threshold is therefore operational rather than purely ontological.

The Dēliņi sash illustrates the distinction. The physical sash is an independently identified heritage entity about which we maintain knowledge. It therefore requires an Item. A photograph showing the sash may initially be only evidence used during review. If the photograph is subsequently selected for publication, independently described, assigned rights information, cited by other resources or used as a persistent digital representation of the sash, it becomes useful to give the photograph independent graph identity as well.

This produces a deliberately selective graph. The graph should contain the entities and relationships needed to operate the Heritage Digital Twin, rather than attempting to reproduce every file and intermediate object created during documentation.

### Digital representations, working files and external evidence
