The demonstrator suggests three practically different treatments of digital resources.

First, some digital resources are **intended to become part of the published Heritage Digital Twin**. For example, we may select a high-quality photograph of the Dēliņi sash for publication. The photograph can then be represented as an HC5 Digital Representation and related to the HC1 heritage entity that it represents [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. Because the photograph itself may have an identifier, creator, creation date, licence, file format and publication status, giving it independent graph identity can be justified.

Second, some digital representations are **published and maintained elsewhere**. An image associated with a record in MuIS, Finna or Garamantas may provide important evidence and a useful access point without becoming a digital object under our control. We may preserve the source and relevant contextual information, for example through a WACZ capture, while continuing to identify the external record or representation through its authoritative URI. Bounded federation allows relevant structured statements from such sources to become candidate claims without requiring us to reproduce the entire external record in our graph.

Third, we have **working resources** created or collected during documentation. Our own photographic workflow, for example, may produce thousands of JPG and RAW files. Some may be blurred, duplicated, accidentally placed in the wrong directory or simply unnecessary for the intended publication. These files can still matter. Their existence, location or use may be relevant to the documentation and maintenance process. Nevertheless, this does not mean that each file should receive a QID.

We therefore distinguish **retention from graph promotion**. A RAW file can be retained as part of the documentation package without becoming a first-class graph entity. A damaged photograph can remain traceable as a resource considered during maintenance even when a data steward decides that it should not be published or used as the preferred representation. Betwixt can record this decision without requiring the rejected or non-promoted resource to occupy the same semantic position as a published digital representation.

This distinction is particularly important for multimodal evidence. The same principle applies to photographs, audio recordings, video, captured web pages and textual documents. The fact that something was used as evidence does not by itself determine whether it should become a persistent node in the public knowledge graph.

### Inspection contexts and overlapping twins

The Dēliņi case also makes it difficult to define the boundary of a Heritage Digital Twin solely by looking at individual objects. During one documentation activity, a curator may inspect the Dēliņi farmstead, enter the farmhouse, photograph the master bedroom, document the sash and bed found there, and consult an archival record concerning the same place. The resulting evidence can support propositions about several related heritage entities.

These entities can participate in different meaningful contexts. The sash can be considered as part of the contents of the farmhouse, as an example of Livonian textile heritage, as an artefact in a museum collection, or as evidence in a study of traditional weaving. The farmhouse can simultaneously be considered as part of the Dēliņi farmstead, an architectural heritage entity, a museum exhibit and a location associated with the documented objects.

We therefore use an **inspection context** as an implementation concept for describing the bounded situation within which evidence was collected and candidate claims were produced. An inspection context can identify the place, collection, activity, research purpose or other practical boundary relevant to a particular documentation process. It helps explain why certain resources and propositions were considered together without asserting that they must permanently belong to one indivisible Heritage Digital Twin.

Inspection context is consequently different from HC1 identity. The same HC1 can participate in several inspection contexts, and one inspection context can involve several HC1 entities. It is also different from HC2: it helps us explain the circumstances under which knowledge entered or changed one or more digital twins rather than defining the twin itself.

This becomes particularly useful when evidence is reused. A photograph originally made while documenting the Dēliņi farmhouse may later provide evidence for a study of Livonian textiles. We should be able to reuse that evidence and the already stabilised knowledge without pretending that the second research context is identical to the first.

We therefore propose **Inspection Context** as an explicit implementation concept for consideration in future HDT-O development. It would represent the bounded curatorial, research or documentation context within which a selected group of heritage entities, representations, evidence and propositions are considered together. It should not replace HC1 or HC2 and should not imply a new part-whole relationship between the participating Heritage Digital Twins.

The Dēliņi demonstrator suggests that such a concept would be particularly useful for practical work with overlapping twins. The same HC1 may participate in several inspection contexts, while one inspection context may involve several HC1 entities and their corresponding HC2 digital twins. Formalising this distinction would allow implementations to record **why these particular entities and resources were examined together** without turning that temporary or purpose-specific scope into an intrinsic boundary of the heritage entities or their digital twins.

### Mereology and relationships between Heritage Digital Twins

The same examples expose a more fundamental question about the relationship between heritage entities and their digital twins. Heritage objects frequently form part-whole structures. The Dēliņi farmstead contains a farmhouse; the farmhouse contains a master bedroom; the bedroom contains a sash and a bed. Depending on the purpose of the digital twin, several of these entities may independently warrant identification and description.

HDT-O permits parts of heritage entities to be treated as heritage entities in their own right [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. This is necessary, but it creates an implementation question when both a whole and its parts have digital twins. If the sash has its own HC2 and the farmhouse has its own HC2, the relationship between the physical entities does not automatically tell us how their digital twins should be related.

We should not assume that the HC2 of the farmhouse simply *contains* the complete HC2 of every object located within it. The digital twin of the farmhouse may contain propositions concerning the sash because those propositions are relevant to understanding the farmhouse. The sash's own digital twin may contain a much richer set of propositions about material, production technique, provenance, conservation and cultural affiliation. The two twins therefore overlap in subject matter without necessarily having a simple part-whole relationship.

The problem becomes even clearer with digital representations. A published photograph can itself be an independently managed digital object while simultaneously representing the sash and documenting the farmhouse interior. It may participate in the digital twins of several heritage entities without being reducible to any one of them.

For our implementation, we therefore keep **mereological relationships between heritage entities** separate from **relationships between their digital twins**. If the sash is physically part of a larger documented context, that relationship belongs to the domain description of the relevant HC1 entities. Which propositions and digital representations are included in the corresponding HC2 structures is determined by the purpose and maintained scope of those twins.

HDT-O already provides **HP3 is digital twin component of** for relationships between HC2 instances, including component relationships that are not limited to physical or geographical part-whole relations [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. The implementation question exposed by Dēliņi is therefore narrower: how should we distinguish relatively persistent digital-twin component relationships from temporary or purpose-specific **inspection contexts** in which several otherwise independent heritage entities and twins are examined together?

We propose that future HDT-O guidance, or a future revision of the ontology, make this distinction explicit. An inspection context would provide a bounded view for research, documentation or review without asserting that every participating HC2 is thereby a component of another HC2.

### Evidence, provenance and normative decisions

The Dēliņi demonstrator finally shows why evidence, domain knowledge and provenance need to remain distinguishable even when they are presented together to a curator.

Consider again the photograph of the tablet-woven sash. Several different statements may be involved:

**this JPG — represents — the sash**

**the sash — instance of — tablet-woven sash**

**the sash — heritage of — Livonians**

The first establishes how a digital resource relates to the heritage entity. The other statements concern the heritage entity itself. If a curator uses the photograph and a museum record to accept these claims, the fact that those resources were consulted, together with the identity of the reviewer and the review activity, belongs to provenance.

Keeping these distinctions explicit allows us to answer different questions later. Domain knowledge can answer **what do we currently claim about the sash?** Provenance can answer **why do we currently accept that claim, on the basis of which evidence, and following which review?**

The distinction becomes even more important when an action is contemplated. Suppose we want to publish the photograph. Knowing that the photograph represents the sash and that the sash is Livonian heritage does not by itself tell us whether the photograph may be published. We may additionally need to know who created the photograph, under which conditions it was created or obtained, whether it depicts an identifiable person, which rights apply, and which organisation has authority to make the publication decision.

We treat these as **normative questions** rather than ordinary descriptive properties of the heritage entity. The relevant decision can depend on stabilised domain knowledge, provenance, an applicable policy and the contemplated action. A rule-based system may then derive a candidate normative conclusion such as *publication permitted*, *publication prohibited* or *human legal review required*.

This is also why a resource that never becomes a public Wikibase Item may still need adequate provenance. A working photograph that is unsuitable for publication may nevertheless have been used during a review. Conversely, a photograph that is technically excellent and correctly linked to an HC1 may still not be publishable because the applicable rights or policy conditions do not permit that action.

The implementation therefore does not collapse **evidence**, **knowledge**, **provenance** and **normative conclusions** into a single set of statements. They interact, but they answer different questions. HDT-O provides an important part of the semantic structure for heritage entities, digital representations, proposition sets and maintenance activities. Our implementation complements this with explicit human review, provenance management and downstream normative inference. This separation allows the digital twin to remain useful for research and federation without treating every accepted descriptive statement as an automatic warrant for subsequent action.

## Implications for HDTO

The Dēliņi demonstrator suggests that HDT-O 1.1 already provides a useful semantic backbone for implementing Heritage Digital Twins. The implementation does not require replacing HDT-O with a separate operational ontology. Rather, it requires a clear division of labour between HDT-O, the operational Wikibase data model, provenance vocabularies, and the review and inference methods described in this tutorial.

At the same time, implementation makes some questions more visible than they are at the conceptual level. In particular, an operational system must decide what receives independent identity, how changing knowledge is maintained, how evidence is connected to the claims established from it, and how several related or overlapping digital twins can reuse the same resources and knowledge. These are not necessarily deficiencies of HDT-O. Some are deliberately outside its scope; others may indicate areas where future versions or implementation guidance could provide greater precision.

### What HDTO 1.1 already models well

The most useful feature of HDT-O for our implementation is the distinction between the **HC1 Heritage Entity** and the **HC2 Heritage Digital Twin** [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. This prevents the digital representation from being confused with the heritage entity itself. The Dēliņi farmhouse remains the heritage entity even as its digital description changes, new photographs are added, erroneous statements are corrected, and new research produces further knowledge.

HDT-O also provides useful specialisations for resources encountered in practical documentation. **HC3 Tangible Heritage Entity** allows physical heritage entities such as buildings and artefacts to be distinguished from their digital representations, while **HC5 Digital Representation** provides a place for digital resources such as photographs [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. This is particularly valuable in a multimodal workflow because a photograph can be represented as a resource in its own right without being confused with the object that it depicts.

The representation of changing knowledge through **HC16 Heritage Proposition Set** is another important strength. An HC2 does not need to be understood as one permanently fixed description. **HP33 contains** identifies proposition sets forming part of the current twin, while **HP34 contained** provides a relationship to former proposition sets [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. This allows the heritage entity to remain stable while the formal knowledge maintained about it changes.

HDT-O 1.1 also provides an explicit maintenance model. **HC11 Digital Twin Maintenance** gives semantic identity to activities that change or complement the twin. **HP18 has documented** and **HP19 has composed** connect such activities to the heritage entity and its digital twin, while **HP30 added content**, **HP31 deleted content** and **HP32 replaced** allow changes in content to be described explicitly [@echoes_hdto_1-1]. This is important for a review-based implementation because correction does not have to mean silently overwriting previous knowledge.

Together, these concepts provide a useful lifecycle:

**HC1 heritage entity → HC2 digital twin → current HC16 proposition content → HC11 maintenance → new HC16 proposition content → updated HC2**

This lifecycle fits well with a Wikibase implementation in which the heritage entity has a stable operational anchor while the knowledge maintained about it can be reviewed, corrected and extended over time.

### What the implementation framework must supply

HDT-O does not by itself determine how evidence becomes accepted knowledge. For an operational Heritage Digital Twin, we therefore need an additional semantic production workflow.

In our implementation this begins with evidence. Photographs, archival records, WACZ captures and external structured data are transformed with R and OpenRefine into candidate claims that can be inspected. Betwixt provides the human review boundary at which these claims can be accepted, rejected or deferred. Only accepted claims enter the stabilised knowledge from which the operational twin is maintained.

The implementation framework must also preserve the distinction between **evidence**, **domain knowledge** and **provenance**. A photograph may provide evidence for the claim that an object is a tablet-woven sash. The proposition **object — instance of — tablet-woven sash** belongs to domain knowledge. The record that a particular curator used that photograph when reviewing the proposition belongs to provenance. These relationships must remain recoverable even when they are presented together in one review interface.

Wikibase supplies the operational graph in which the resulting knowledge can be maintained. Its data model provides Items, ItemDescriptions, Properties and Statements [@wikibase_datamodel]. Our mapping determines how these operational structures are interpreted when expressed as an HDT-O Heritage Digital Twin. This mapping deliberately avoids requiring a separate Q-item for every HDT-O entity.

The implementation must therefore also supply **identity and graph-promotion rules**. A heritage entity that must be independently maintained normally requires stable graph identity. A published photograph may require independent identity because it has its own provenance, rights and persistent relationships. A working RAW file may remain an identified resource in the documentation package without becoming a Q-item. Similarly, HC11 maintenance activities and HC16 proposition sets can be represented systematically from review and provenance records where independent Wikibase Item identity is unnecessary.

The implementation framework additionally supplies the rules governing **semantic inference**. Stabilised knowledge can be used as input to explicit inference rules or symbolic AI, but inferred results are treated as new candidate claims rather than automatically becoming accepted knowledge. Where human scrutiny is required, they return to the same review process.

Finally, the implementation must support **normative inference** separately from domain inference. A descriptive claim that a photograph depicts a particular heritage entity does not imply that the photograph may be published, disclosed or federated. Normative conclusions require the relevant stabilised knowledge, provenance, applicable policy and contemplated action. HDT-O can provide important inputs to this process without requiring the Heritage Digital Twin ontology itself to become a complete policy language.

The resulting architecture therefore assigns different responsibilities to complementary components:

**HDT-O → what the Heritage Digital Twin and its principal components mean**

**Wikibase → where operational structured knowledge is identified, maintained and queried**

**R and OpenRefine → how heterogeneous evidence and external data are prepared and reconciled**

**Betwixt → how candidate claims are exposed to human review and review provenance is captured**

**explicit inference rules → how new domain and normative candidate claims are derived**

The purpose of this division is not to extend HDT-O until it describes every part of the technical system. It is to preserve HDT-O as the semantic model of the Heritage Digital Twin while making its concepts operational in a reproducible workflow.

### Questions for further development of HDTO

The implementation nevertheless identifies several questions that may be useful for further development of HDT-O or for accompanying implementation guidance.

The first concerns **inspection context and the boundary of a Heritage Digital Twin**. HDT-O already provides HP3 for relationships between digital-twin components, but practical documentation also creates temporary and purpose-specific groupings that should not necessarily be interpreted as component relationships. A sash may be examined in the context of a farmhouse interior, a museum collection or a study of Livonian textiles without each inspection context redefining the identity or permanent composition of its HC2. We therefore recommend considering an explicit **Inspection Context** concept in future HDT-O development or implementation guidance to represent why particular heritage entities, twins, representations and evidence were considered together for a particular purpose.

A related question concerns **mereology**. Physical heritage entities can have parts, and those parts may themselves be heritage entities. However, the relationship between HC1 entities does not necessarily imply the same relationship between their HC2 digital twins. If the Dēliņi farmhouse has a digital twin and the sash inside it has another digital twin, the sash's HC2 should not necessarily become a literal part of the farmhouse's HC2. The two twins may instead share propositions, representations or references for particular purposes. A clearer account of relationships between the twins of related heritage entities would help implementations avoid reproducing physical mereology mechanically in the digital layer.

A third question concerns **digital representations and graph identity**. In practice, documentation can produce thousands of photographs, RAW files, web captures and intermediate resources. HDT-O can describe digital representations, but an implementation still needs to determine which resources warrant persistent semantic identity. Guidance distinguishing published representations, externally maintained representations and internal working resources would make large-scale implementation more predictable.

A fourth question concerns **evidence and the formation of propositions**. HDTO provides a strong model for proposition sets and Digital Twin Maintenance, but our implementation needs to know more specifically which evidence was used to establish or review individual claims. This becomes especially important when several pieces of evidence support or contradict the same proposition. Further alignment with explicit provenance and evidence models could clarify this relationship without requiring evidence itself to be treated as accepted domain knowledge.

A fifth question concerns the **granularity of HC16 Heritage Proposition Sets**. In an operational system, claims may be reviewed and changed individually, while HC16 represents a persistent set of propositions whose identity depends on its complete content. The implementation question is therefore how independently reviewed statement-level changes should be packaged into successive HC16 proposition sets, and when a newly produced HC16 should replace rather than simply supplement an existing proposition set. Implementation guidance would be particularly valuable for systems such as Wikibase, where statements can change independently while HDT-O proposition sets are persistent objects.

Finally, the implementation raises the question of the boundary between **descriptive knowledge and action**. A Heritage Digital Twin can contain increasingly rich knowledge about an entity and its digital representations, but this knowledge should not automatically be interpreted as permission to publish, reuse, disclose or federate those resources. Rights and policy reasoning may therefore be best treated as a complementary normative layer that consumes selected HDT-O knowledge and provenance rather than being folded indiscriminately into the descriptive model.

These questions do not undermine the usefulness of HDT-O 1.1. On the contrary, they become visible because its central distinctions are sufficiently concrete to implement. The Dēliņi demonstrator suggests that **HC1/HC2 identity, HC16 proposition content and HC11 maintenance already provide a workable core for an operational Heritage Digital Twin**. The remaining challenge is to define disciplined interfaces between that core and the processes through which evidence is reviewed, knowledge is stabilised, related twins are federated, and decisions about subsequent actions are made.
